newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norwegian crown undeterred by official rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Norwegian crown undeterred by official rate cut.

text.p: The Norwegian crown, undeterred by a cut in official interest rates, powered to its strongest level in more than six years on Thursday on what dealers described as speculative buying.
Short-term swap rates also fell to add pressure on the central bank which announced the cuts on Wednesday in a fruitless effort to curb the steady rise of the oil currency.

Analysts say the crown is undervalued as the Norwegian economy is booming with huge surpluses in the national budget and current account. Norway is the world's second biggest oil exporter after Saudi Arabia.

"Foreign buyers have discovered that the strong Norwegian economy is in a unique situation compared to other countries in Europe," said Eirik Larsen, senior currency analyst at Den norske Bank. "The bank cut the rates but the market reacted by buying more crowns. This pressure will keep up in 1997."
"The rate cut fuelled speculative buying," said one dealer.

Effective Thursday, the central bank trimmed the overnight deposit rate for commercial and savings banks to 3.5 percent from 4.0 percent. The overnight lending rate was reduced to 5.5 percent from 6.0 percent.

But the crown on Thursday outperformed the inverse ECU index of European currencies for the first time. It appreciated from 100.64 on the index shortly before the cut was announced after Norwegian markets closed on Wednesday to 99.89 when they shut on Thursday.
"The Norwegian crown is now stronger than it has ever been since we linked it to the ECU in October, 1990," Leif Eide, head of market operations at the central bank, told Reuters.
Players said the 50 basis-point cut had been discounted because the market had expected another cut after similar rate reductions on November 6 failed to hold back the crown.
Now they are waiting for yet another cut in official rates.

"The fundamentals are still good, nobody's taking profit, it can only move one way and that's up," said one dealer. "If you look at the (yield) curve at the short end you can see the market has already discounted another rate cut of about 25 basis points."

The three-month eurokrone swap rate, fixed at 3.66 percent shortly before Wednesday's announcement, fell to 3.38 percent at 1500 GMT on Thursday -- below the deposit rate's new official floor of 3.5 percent.
This meant that banks can continue borrowing money from each other and deposit them at a premium in the central bank.
To counter the appreciation since the cut two months ago, the bank has bought foreign currency worth 38 billion crowns, including 15 billion crowns since the beginning of this year.
The central bank has been hesitant to cut rates because such a move could fuel inflation and overheat the economy.

"The government will have to decide whether to maintain a stable crown at all costs or if it should allow the crown to grow as strong as it should be," Larsen said. "That is the political question to ask now."

The primary objective of Norwegian monetary policy is exchange rate stability. The crown is in a dirty float, which means the central bank intervenes to maintain a level that is not officially declared.
The Finance Ministry forecast on November 29 that inflation would be 2.5 percent this year, up from 1.25 percent in 1996.
